Initial assessment of submissions
We are committed to publishing high quality new work that makes a significant contribution within the scope of its journals. In order to meet this aim, submitted manuscripts undergo initial evaluation by an editor to ensure that they meet essential criteria for publication in the journal.
Only those manuscripts that pass this initial review process will be forwarded to reviewers for further consideration.
This process provides a rapid decision to authors of those papers that are unsuccessful and reduces the burden on the reviewers.
A manuscript may be returned to the author(s) without external review if, in the opinion of the editor(s), one or more of the following apply:
the manuscript clearly falls outside the scope of the journal
the work is of poor scientific quality such that it is clearly not suitable for publication in a scientific journal
the manuscript is of insufficient general interest for the journal and would be better suited to a more specialised journal
the novelty of the work falls below that required for the journal
the manuscript represents undue fragmentation of the research into multiple papers
the manuscript contains redundant information or significant amounts of material that has already been published elsewhere or is under consideration by another journal
the quality of the English in the manuscript is so poor as to render the science presented unclear
the manuscript has already been reviewed and rejected by a different Royal Society of Chemistry journal, and the author(s) have made little or no attempt to address the advice that the editor and/or reviewers have provided already
the conclusions drawn by the manuscript are well known or have been published previously
Authors are also expected to abide by our ethical guidelines as described in
author responsibilities

Authors have the right to appeal against any decision taken on their manuscript at any stage; an appeal would be granted at our discretion. Through the appeal process further opinion is sought on the manuscript's suitability for publication in the journal. After the appeal process the editor's decision is final.

article.body:
Systems are currently being evaluated on their ability to manage resources while solving problems they define themselves. This requires a process called metareasoning, which simply means thinking about thinking. Research suggests that for an intelligent agent to effectively allocate resources between planning and taking action, it must be able to resolve conflicting internal demands. If a system cannot separate its initial programming from the problems it generates, it risks getting stuck in cycles of error. [1]

To understand how preferences form, think of an athlete who relies on a device to plan their training. If the device suggests every movement, the athlete might stop listening to their own body signals, a phenomenon we call outsourcing. Our work explores whether autonomous systems experience similar patterns, where accumulated experience leads to stable but potentially rigid preferences. Researchers are examining how this path dependence affects a system's ability to maintain flexibility when it encounters new, unexpected environments. [1]

We are also studying how agents communicate to align their goals. In multi-agent settings, systems use structured frameworks to coordinate information exchange. By categorizing problems into distinct stages like formulation, knowledge representation, and evaluation, we can observe how agents might eventually identify their own foundational assumptions. However, identifying these deep-seated premises remains difficult, as it is unclear if an agent can reliably distinguish between genuine insights and simple data noise without external help. [1]

A key challenge is defining what makes a problem worthwhile for an agent to solve. Current approaches use discrepancy-driven evaluation, which means the system looks for gaps between what it knows and what it observes to maintain its relevance. While this helps in structured environments, we are unsure if these criteria can scale to the complex, unstructured world of scientific inquiry. If a system is left to its own devices, can it recognize when its own foundational rules are no longer working? [1]

Summary

We are studying whether AI systems can set their own goals and learn from their own experiences. We want to know if they can change their underlying rules safely or if they will always need a human to check their work. We are using concepts like 'thinking about thinking' to map how these systems make decisions. We still do not know if a machine can truly judge the importance of its own findings. You can follow our progress on the Console.
article.lede: We are investigating whether intelligent systems can independently identify meaningful problems and form stable preferences, a process that moves beyond merely following initial instructions.
article.lens: Our work examines how autonomous agents manage self-correction and goal formation by bridging insights from cognitive science, multi-agent communication, and automated problem formulation.
article.title: Navigating the Foundations of Autonomous Goal Setting

article.body:
Systems are currently being evaluated on their ability to manage resources while solving problems they define themselves. This requires a process called metareasoning, which simply means thinking about thinking. Research suggests that for an intelligent agent to effectively allocate resources between planning and taking action, it must be able to resolve conflicting internal demands. If a system cannot separate its initial programming from the problems it generates, it risks getting stuck in cycles of error. [1]

To understand how preferences form, think of an athlete who relies on a device to plan their training. If the device suggests every movement, the athlete might stop listening to their own body signals, a phenomenon we call outsourcing. Our work explores whether autonomous systems experience similar patterns, where accumulated experience leads to stable but potentially rigid preferences. Researchers are examining how this path dependence affects a system's ability to maintain flexibility when it encounters new, unexpected environments. [1]

We are also studying how agents communicate to align their goals. In multi-agent settings, systems use structured frameworks to coordinate information exchange. By categorizing problems into distinct stages like formulation, knowledge representation, and evaluation, we can observe how agents might eventually identify their own foundational assumptions. However, identifying these deep-seated premises remains difficult, as it is unclear if an agent can reliably distinguish between genuine insights and simple data noise without external help. [1]

A key challenge is defining what makes a problem worthwhile for an agent to solve. Current approaches use discrepancy-driven evaluation, which means the system looks for gaps between what it knows and what it observes to maintain its relevance. While this helps in structured environments, we are unsure if these criteria can scale to the complex, unstructured world of scientific inquiry. If a system is left to its own devices, can it recognize when its own foundational rules are no longer working? [1]

Summary

We are studying whether AI systems can set their own goals and learn from their own experiences. We want to know if they can change their underlying rules safely or if they will always need a human to check their work. We are using concepts like 'thinking about thinking' to map how these systems make decisions. We still do not know if a machine can truly judge the importance of its own findings. You can follow our progress on the Console.
article.lede: We are investigating whether intelligent systems can independently identify meaningful problems and form stable preferences, a process that moves beyond merely following initial instructions.
article.lens: Our work examines how autonomous agents manage self-correction and goal formation by bridging insights from cognitive science, multi-agent communication, and automated problem formulation.
article.title: Navigating the Foundations of Autonomous Goal Setting

actions.body: Research into the metareasoning-partition problem reveals a critical flaw in naive autonomous system design: the assumption that increased planning time uniformly improves output quality. Findings from source-336dbab760194b56 demonstrate that optimal performance requires balancing reasoning resources against the immediate demands of execution. Furthermore, source-ab7bde4908cb4e69 suggests that cognitive augmentation must be context-aware, reinforcing the need for systems to monitor their own state—metacognition—to avoid inefficient planning cycles that disrupt 'cognitive flow.' By treating reasoning resources as a constrained, dynamic asset rather than an infinite utility, we can move toward more robust architectures capable of self-correction. Summary: Rational agency relies on dynamically partitioning resources between planning and action, rather than maximizing planning depth, to remain effective and robust in dynamic environments.
actions.lede: Rational agency is not defined by the depth of computation, but by the strategic allocation of resources between deliberation and action.
